**Module 02 Slice 3 (sync pipeline §4.1 DB-writing orchestration) —
genuinely done: coded, tested, security-reviewed (PASS, mandatory per
this slice's own dispatch since it decrypts credentials and writes real
financial data via service-role), QA-reviewed (PASS). See the full
review writeup further below.** This is the first slice
in Module 02 where `trades`/`trade_fills`/`trade_events`/`blocks`/`fills`/
`sync_runs`/`coverage_gaps` rows actually get written for real, gluing
Slices 1-2's pure functions (`blocks.ts`/`grouping.ts`/`trade-facts.ts`)
into one DB-writing pipeline.

- `lib/ingestion/sync.ts` — `runSync(accountId, adapter, options)`. Total
  for every `trading_accounts.platform` (never throws for a manual
  account — returns `{ skipped: true, reason: 'manual_account' }`, since
  §4.8 manual entry has no credential and doesn't sync through this path
  at all). Runs entirely under `withServiceRoleConnection` (this is a
  trusted backend process, not a client request, per the dispatch), every
  query explicitly scoped to the one `accountId`/`userId` in play. Writes
  a real `sync_runs` row (`ok | partial | failed`, `fills_seen`,
  `fills_new`, `window_from/to`, `tier`, `trigger`, `error_code`) on every
  call, including failures (credential/adapter/KMS errors all map to a
  named `SyncErrorCode` rather than throwing past the caller).
- **Judgment calls made reconciling §4.1's prose into code (all
  documented in `sync.ts`'s own header comment, per this slice's
  dispatch instruction — flagged here for visibility, not repeated in
  full):**
  1. Overlap window default: 6 hours (`DEFAULT_OVERLAP_MS`), inside the
     dispatch's own suggested 1-24h range, overridable.
  2. `since` on an account's first-ever sync (no prior `sync_runs` row):
     `trading_accounts.connected_at` (falling back to `created_at`), no
     overlap subtraction (nothing to overlap against yet).
  3. Coverage-gap detection (step 5): any positive gap between
     `window_from` and the earliest returned fill is recorded — EXCEPT on
     an account's first-ever sync, which is deliberately EXEMPT. This
     exemption is a real correctness fix found while testing, not just a
     judgment call: without it, `window_from = connected_at` (routinely
     well before a brand-new account's first real trade) would make
     EVERY first sync of EVERY account falsely report a coverage gap the
     moment it found its first fill — a false positive on the common
     case, not the rare one.
  4. **Block/trade recompute scope (steps 6-9) — the single biggest scope
     decision in this slice.** An (account, instrument) span that already
     has ANY matching `blocks` row (matched by exact `opened_at` instant)
     is left COMPLETELY UNTOUCHED on resync — no write of any kind,
     confirmed or not. Only genuinely brand-new blocks (no existing row
     at all) are derived, grouped, and written. This trivially and
     unambiguously satisfies "never touch a confirmed trade" (nothing
     pre-existing is ever touched, full stop), at the real, deliberate
     cost of NOT implementing "append new fills to an already-open
     unconfirmed block across a resync boundary" in this slice — a
     genuine, known limitation, not silently dropped. Building that
     safely turned out to be a much larger feature than it first looked:
     `trades`' own delete trigger (ADR 0011) makes ANY trade backed by a
     real (non-`manual:`) fill permanently non-deletable regardless of
     `confirmed_at`, so "recompute" can never mean "delete and re-derive
     from scratch" for a real account the way the pure
     `groupBlock`/`deriveBlocks` functions do in isolation — a real,
     in-place, matching/updating regrouping algorithm is separate,
     larger future work. When a matched existing block's freshly
     recomputed fill membership includes fills not yet reflected in its
     stored trade(s), that's detected and surfaced in the result's
     `anomalies` array (+ `console.warn`) as `FILL_LATE_ARRIVAL`
     (confirmed block — §9's own named error code) or
     `BLOCK_EXTENSION_DEFERRED` (unconfirmed, just out of scope) — never
     a silent rewrite either way.

- `lib/ingestion/arm-matching.ts` — the pure `match(arm, fills)` decision
  from §4.5's pseudocode (`matchArmEvent`), no DB access, same posture as
  `grouping.ts`/`trade-facts.ts`. Five judgment calls reconciling §4.5's
  prose into code, all documented in the file's own header (full detail
  there): (1) "candidates" is read as candidate ENTRY FILLS, literally
  per the pseudocode's own `role = 'entry'` clause, but since an entry
  fill maps 1:1 to its trade, this is equivalent to "candidate trades
  identified by their entry fill" — both readings reconciled, not
  competing; (2) the spec names outcomes for 0-candidates-window-expired
  (`never_filled`), 1 (`matched`), and >1 (`ambiguous`) but says nothing
  about 0-candidates-window-still-open — read as "no state change, stays
  `pending`" per 00-foundation §6.2's silence principle, matching
  `arm_events.match_state`'s own DDL default; (3) the window boundary
  ("between armed_at and armed_at + WINDOW") is a closed interval on both
  ends; (4) side/direction matching reuses `trade-facts.ts`'s exact
  buy→long/sell→short mapping, one canonical definition, not a second
  parallel one; (5) `WINDOW` default 30 min, overridable.
- `lib/ingestion/trade-captures.ts` — `writeTradeCapture`/
  `lockPreEntryCaptures`, the pre-entry lock (§4.5's second paragraph,
  §4.7's "Edit pre-entry captures: Never after lock"). Real design
  finding recorded in the file's own header: `trade_captures`' primary
  key is `(trade_id, field_id)` only — NOT `(trade_id, field_id, moment)`
  — so there is exactly one row per field per trade ever, which makes
  "never after lock" enforceable as a flat reject-on-conflict rather than
  a versioned append: once a `(trade_id, field_id)` row exists with
  `moment = 'pre_entry'`, every later write attempt for that same pair is
  rejected outright (`{ applied: false, reason: 'pre_entry_locked' }`),
  never silently overwritten. This is also the one general write path any
  FUTURE `trade_captures` writer (Module 03/06's capture UI) should route
  through — nothing else writes to this table yet in this repo, so there
  was nothing to retrofit.

**Module 02 Slice 5 (confirm/freeze transaction §4.6) — coder pass
complete, real functionality against the real live DB, not stubs.

- `lib/ingestion/confirm.ts` — `confirmDay(accountId, serverDay, options)`
  (the user-initiated confirm/freeze transaction for ONE account/day) and
  `autoConfirmStaleTrades(options)` (the daily 7-day sweep), both running
  as a single `withServiceRoleConnection` transaction each, matching
  `sync.ts`'s established pattern (every query explicitly scoped to the
  account/user resolved from the loaded account row, per ADR 0005's
  caveat). `confirmDay` implements §4.6's three assertions literally:
  no unresolved `coverage_gaps` row overlapping the server_day, no
  `grouping_confidence = 'ambiguous'` trade anywhere in the day, and — this
  slice's own required extension, not literal spec text — no eligible
  trade's backing block has a fill not yet reflected in its derived facts
  (`sync.ts`'s own `BLOCK_EXTENSION_DEFERRED`/`FILL_LATE_ARRIVAL`
  anomalies, previously only logged and ignored). Refusals are a
  structured, typed, discriminated-union result
  (`ConfirmDayResult`/`code`/per-code detail), never a thrown generic
  string; a genuine caller bug (unknown `accountId`, zero trade rows with
  no explicit `kind` override) throws a named error class instead, same
  split `sync.ts` already established between "legitimate but blocked"
  and "caller bug."
- **This is the mechanism that closes the tracked BLOCK_EXTENSION_DEFERRED
  gap Slice 3/4's tester pass flagged as "a firm requirement, not just a
  'revisit if it becomes a blocker'":** rather than building in-place
  block extension (still out of scope, a genuinely larger feature), a
  stuck-open/stale-facts trade can now also never be silently CONFIRMED
  with incomplete facts — both `confirmDay` and `autoConfirmStaleTrades`
  refuse/skip it instead. `lib/ingestion/sync.ts` was refactored (no
  behavior change, all 26 existing unit + 11 live tests still pass
  unmodified) to factor the "does this block's fresh fill membership agree
  with what's recorded" check out of `recomputeInstrument` into a shared,
  exported `loadInstrumentBlockState`/`findUnrecordedBlockFills`/
  `findUnrecordedFillsForBlock` — the literal same correctness question,
  now asked once, not duplicated.
- `lib/ingestion/server-day.ts` — new `computeServerDayRange(serverDay,
  dayRollover)`, the documented inverse of `computeServerDay` (needed
  because `coverage_gaps` stores UTC instant ranges but `trades.server_day`
  is a plain date, and there's no column carrying the instant range a
  server_day covers). Two-pass IANA-zone-aware wall-clock→UTC conversion
  (`localWallClockToUtc`), verified algebraically against the fixture
  README's own reverse formula, then confirmed by a full round-trip
  property test (200 runs × 5 rollover shapes, `fast-check`) AND against
  every real fill in all 8 golden fixtures.
- **Judgment calls made reconciling §4.6's prose into code (full detail in
  `confirm.ts`'s own header comment, summarized in the decision log
  below):** (1) the coverage-gap overlap test's own derivation; (2) the
  ambiguous-grouping assertion scans every trade in the day, not just the
  confirmation-eligible subset — an ambiguous OPEN trade would otherwise
  slip past on a technicality; (3) the stale-block guard's existence and
  scope (this slice's own extension of §4.6, not literal text); (4)
  `day_closeouts.kind` defaults to `'traded'` whenever the day has ANY
  trade row (even if all already confirmed — a legitimate idempotent
  re-confirm), and is a required, explicit caller error only when the day
  has ZERO trade rows of any status and no override was supplied; (5) the
  day_closeouts insert is `ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING`, genuinely
  idempotent, documented why (a stray trade landing between a page reload
  and a second click).
- **`autoConfirmStaleTrades` — two judgment calls flagged explicitly for
  the decision log, per the dispatch's own request:**
  1. **Never inserts a `day_closeouts` row, full stop** — read literally
     from §4.6's "gets a day_closeouts row only if the user closed it
     out." `day_closeouts` rows are created EXCLUSIVELY by `confirmDay`
     (the only INSERT statement into this table in the whole repo). An
     alternative reading ("insert one anyway, just never counted toward
     the streak") was considered and rejected — it would require either a
     new column speculatively invented ahead of Module 07 existing to
     define what it means, or overloading `confirmed_by = 'auto_7d'` on
     `day_closeouts` itself, a decision better left to whichever slice
     actually builds the streak.
  2. **The stale/incomplete-block guard IS applied to auto-confirm too,**
     reasoned through rather than skipped: a `status = 'closed'` trade
     (the only kind ever eligible for auto-confirm) can still share its
     block with an already-CONFIRMED sibling trade (§4.3: "a block is the
     upper bound on a trade, not the answer" — one block can host
     multiple trades), and a late fill on that shared block is exactly
     `sync.ts`'s `FILL_LATE_ARRIVAL` case. Applied as a PER-TRADE skip
     (`tradesSkippedStaleBlock`), not a whole-sweep refusal — this sweep
     spans every account/user in one call, so failing the entire batch
     over one trade's stale block would have a far wider blast radius than
     `confirmDay`'s own per-day scope justifies. **A third guard, beyond
     the literal dispatch, added and flagged here rather than silently
     included:** `autoConfirmStaleTrades`'s eligibility query also
     excludes `grouping_confidence = 'ambiguous'` trades — nothing in
     §4.6's own sentence mentions this, but auto-confirming an ambiguous
     trade would silently freeze rule evaluations (once Module 04 exists)
     over facts the product hasn't decided are correct yet, the same
     freeze-honesty failure mode the stale-block guard exists to prevent.

  assertion) — reasoning is sound, endorsed.** Refusing to confirm a
  trade whose backing block has an unrecorded fill genuinely prevents an
  irreversible harm (a frozen `rule_evaluation`/adherence fact that can
  never be recomputed once Module 04 exists, per AGENTS.md's own
  non-negotiable) in exchange for a recoverable one (a trade sitting
  unconfirmed). That asymmetry — permanent corruption vs. temporary
  inconvenience — is exactly what §9's "silence over wrongness" exists
  to enforce, and this slice applies it correctly to a case §4.6's
  literal text doesn't mention. **Confirmed the flagged consequence is
  real and already honestly documented, not glossed over:** there is no
  way in this repo today to distinguish "stale, more fills genuinely
  still coming" from "stale forever, a data anomaly" — a trade can sit
  `status: 'closed'`, `confirmed_at: null` indefinitely with no path
  back into the lifecycle until Slice 6 (manual split/join) or a future
  in-place block-extension feature exists. The coder already wrote this
  up explicitly in both `confirm.ts`'s own header and a new
  `docs/runbook.md` entry ("Trades stuck unable to confirm —
  coverage-gap / block-anomaly backlog") that names the exact same risk

  (its own dedicated test skips a stale-block trade and reports it in
  `tradesSkippedStaleBlock`, never silently auto-confirms it) — same

  and specifically endorse flagging `autoConfirmStaleTrades`'s
  unscoped, cross-account/cross-user sweep as a genuinely new shape of

  caller in this codebase (per ADR 0005's own caveat) filters explicitly

  takes NO scoping parameter at all and legitimately touches every
  account/user in one call — safe as currently written (the UPDATE only
  ever targets ids its own prior SELECT produced under the service role,
  never a caller-supplied id), but its own function signature offers
  **zero built-in protection** if a future slice ever wires it to a
  route reachable by anything other than a genuinely trusted cron/system
  context — there is no parameter, no internal check, nothing to prevent
  an accidentally-exposed endpoint from triggering a full cross-user
  sweep. Recommend the security reviewer treat "verify the eventual
  trigger surface (Slice 6/7+) enforces service/cron-only invocation,

  found: `confirmDay`'s per-trade UPDATE had no atomic guard (`WHERE id
  = $1 AND account_id = $2`, no `status = 'closed' AND confirmed_at IS
  NULL`), so two genuinely concurrent calls could both "win," leaving
  `confirmed_at`/`confirmed_by` as whichever transaction committed last
  — the same bug shape as an earlier real FAIL in
  `lib/privacy/erasure.ts` (`executeErasure`'s non-atomic
  pending→processing transition). Provided the exact fix, mirroring
  `markDataRequestProcessing`'s pattern. Fixed by the orchestrator in
  both places: (1) `confirmDay`'s per-trade UPDATE, adding `and status =
  'closed' and confirmed_at is null`, only pushing to `tradesConfirmed`
  when `rowCount > 0`; (2) `autoConfirmStaleTrades`'s bulk UPDATE, which
  turned out to have a second, distinct bug beyond the race — without
  the same guard, a trade a concurrent `confirmDay` call had already
  confirmed as `'user'` could get silently overwritten to `'auto_7d'`,
  corrupting confirmation provenance, not just racing on who "wins."
  Fixed with the same guard plus `returning id` so the function only
  reports rows it actually touched. Updated the existing race regression
  test to assert exactly one winner/one empty-list loser (was
  previously proving the bug, now proves the fix), and added a new
  regression test racing `confirmDay` against `autoConfirmStaleTrades`
  directly for the provenance-corruption scenario specifically (the
  re-review noted no dedicated test existed for it). Re-reviewed: PASS —
  independently confirmed correct Postgres READ-COMMITTED semantics in
  both locations, confirmed the additional provenance fix was correctly
  reasoned (not invented busywork), confirmed both regression tests are
  real and would fail against the pre-fix code. Every other area

independently live-tested, 2026-08-22. Security-reviewer and QA passes

- `lib/ingestion/split-join.ts` — `splitTrade(userId, tradeId,
  splitAtFillId)` and `joinTrades(userId, tradeIdA, tradeIdB)`, both
  reusing `grouping.ts`'s `assignRoles` (now exported, no behavior change)
  and `trade-facts.ts`'s `computeTradeFacts` unchanged — "recomputes
  facts" means literally calling the same functions the sync pipeline
  calls, no parallel logic. `lib/ingestion/grouping.ts`'s `assignRoles`
  export is the only change to a previously-reviewed file in this slice.
- **Two-phase write, same `withUserConnection` → `withServiceRoleConnection`
  pattern `manual-entry.ts`/`confirm.ts` already established** — but with
  one deliberate improvement: phase 1 here is PURE VALIDATION (no writes at
  all), so unlike `manual-entry.ts`'s own documented "orphaned-fills
  window" gap, this slice has no analogous partial-write risk — every
  mutation for both functions happens inside phase 2's own single
  transaction, so a mid-operation failure rolls back everything phase 2
  attempted, leaving the pre-operation state completely intact. Phase 2
  re-validates ownership/freeze/boundary-membership from scratch (closes
  the narrow race where a concurrent `confirmDay`/`autoConfirmStaleTrades`
  freezes the trade between phase 1 committing and phase 2 starting).
- **`joinTrades`' delete-trigger interaction — the one genuinely fragile
  mechanism in this slice, exactly as dispatched:** the absorbed trade's
  `trade_fills`/`trade_events` rows are reassigned onto the surviving trade
  FIRST, then the absorbed trade row is deleted, in the SAME phase-2
  transaction — so `forbid_broker_confirmed_trade_delete`'s exists-check
  (evaluated against CURRENT membership, not history) finds nothing backing
  the absorbed trade and permits the delete regardless of whether it was
  originally broker-originated. Proven with a dedicated live test using
  REAL (non-`manual:`) provider-ref fills, not reasoned about only — see
  `__tests__/split-join.live.test.ts`'s join happy-path test, which
  deliberately uses broker-shaped provider refs for exactly this reason,
  plus a second dedicated test exercising the `trade_events` reassignment
  branch specifically (a survivor carrying an ADR-0001 synthetic
  flip-opening entry, built from the real `flip_no_flat` golden fixture via
  `runSync`).
- **Judgment calls made (logged here per 00-foundation §12, full reasoning
  in `split-join.ts`'s own header — none deviate from a stated
  00-foundation convention, so no new ADR was written; flagged for
  security-reviewer/QA to confirm that judgment, not decided unilaterally
  as final):**
  1. Both resulting trades' `grouping_confidence` → `'confident_single'`,
     `grouping_signals` cleared to `{}` — "a user-directed
     split/join has no ambiguity left by definition" (this slice's own
     dispatch, verbatim).
  2. `grouping_source`: `'user_split'` for both trades a split produces
     (§4.7's literal value); `'user_join'` for a join's survivor — both
     verified against `trades_grouping_source_check`'s exact allowed list
     before use.
  3. `ambiguity_resolved_at` set to the operation's own timestamp on every
     trade touched, regardless of prior confidence — read as "the last
     time a human decided this trade's own boundary."
  4. Split boundary validation exactly as dispatched: not a current member
     → `SplitBoundaryNotMemberError`; the ADR-0001 synthetic flip-opening
     entry → `SplitBoundaryIsSyntheticEntryError`; the chronologically-first
     member (and not synthetic) → `SplitBoundaryIsFirstMemberError`. The
     synthetic check is deliberately ordered BEFORE the first-member check
     — a real synthetic entry is always a trade's own first member (proved
     in the file's header), so checking index-zero first would make the
     more specific, more informative error permanently unreachable.
  5. Join's surviving trade: the chronologically-earlier one (`opened_at`),
     tying on `id` for a fully deterministic choice — this slice's own

  6. A known, accepted, explicitly-flagged (not silently swept)

     dispatched, no more — a pathological user-chosen split boundary that
     makes a subset cross net-flat more than once has no additional
     restriction added beyond what was asked, since `assignRoles` itself

**Module 02 Slice 6b — independent `retrospeq-tester` pass, 2026-08-22.**
Read Module 02 §4.7 in full, `split-join.ts` in full including its header
(all 6 judgment calls), and `__tests__/split-join.live.test.ts` in full.
This was a genuine re-derivation, not a re-read of the coder's own claims:

- **Delete-trigger workaround (the highest-priority item) — independently
  verified safe, not just plausible.** Traced `joinTrades`' phase 2 body
  line-by-line against `withServiceRoleConnection`'s implementation
  (`lib/supabase/direct.ts`'s `withRole`): a single Postgres client, one
  `BEGIN`...`COMMIT` per call, every `client.query(...)` call in the
  reassignment `for` loop and the trailing `DELETE` is `await`ed in
  sequence on that same client before the transaction commits — there is
  no async-ordering gap, no missing `await`, no second connection that
  could race it. Cross-checked `forbid_broker_confirmed_trade_delete`'s
  actual SQL (`20260822010000_ingestion_schema.sql` lines 262-275): it is
  a plain `exists(...)` against current `trade_fills`/`trade_events`
  membership at delete-time, exactly as documented, with no history
  tracking to defeat. The coder's own live test ("happy path + the
  delete-trigger interaction") is a real adversarial proof, not a weaker
  stand-in: both trades in that test are seeded with real, non-`manual:`
  provider refs (`join-a-entry`/`join-a-exit`/`join-b-entry`/`join-b-exit`),
  the ABSORBED trade (`tradeB`, the later one) is specifically the one
  carrying broker-shaped refs, and the test asserts both that the absorbed
  trade row is gone (`count = 0`) AND that its underlying `fills` rows
  still exist untouched — i.e. it proves the trigger's actual protected
  invariant ("no broker-originated financial fact is destroyed") holds,
  not merely that the delete didn't throw. A second dedicated live test
  proves the `trade_events` (not just `trade_fills`) reassignment branch
  fires, via a real ADR-0001 synthetic flip-opening entry driven through
  `runSync`. **Independent judgment: this mechanism is sound.** It relies
  on a real, cited property of the trigger (current-membership-only
  check) rather than a coincidence, the reassign-then-delete ordering is
  transaction-atomic (a mid-loop failure rolls back everything, per
  `withRole`'s catch/rollback), and the two live tests exercise exactly
  the dangerous path (real broker-shaped refs, on the absorbed side)
  rather than a weakened `manual:`-prefixed stand-in.
- **Split boundary validation — independently exercised, one gap found
  and closed.** All three named refusal cases (`SplitTradeAlreadyConfirmedError`,
  `SplitBoundaryIsFirstMemberError`, `SplitBoundaryIsSyntheticEntryError`
  via a real `flip_no_flat`-derived trade through `runSync`) are genuine
  live-DB tests, not unit-level logic checks. Found one real gap per the
  dispatch's own prompt ("what if `splitAtFillId` doesn't belong to the
  trade at all"): the existing `SplitBoundaryNotMemberError` test only
  used a syntactically-valid-but-nonexistent UUID, never a REAL fill id
  that belongs to a different trade. Functionally this is the same code
  path (`rows.findIndex` over the target trade's own member rows returns
  -1 either way — confirmed by reading `loadAndValidateSplit`), so it was
  not a correctness bug, but it was a materially weaker proof of the
  adversarial case the dispatch specifically asked about. **Added**
  `lib/ingestion/__tests__/split-join.live.test.ts`'s new test "refuses a
  fill id that is REAL but belongs to a different trade entirely" — seeds
  two independent real trades for the same user, attempts to split trade A
  at a real, currently-backing fill id that belongs to trade B, asserts
  `SplitBoundaryNotMemberError` and that neither trade's `trade_fills` rows
  changed (`count = 4` across both, unchanged). Passes.
- **Role re-derivation correctness — hand-verified arithmetically, both
  operations, matches golden-fixture-review rigor.** Split happy path (4
  fills: buy 50000@1.10000, buy 50000@1.09900, sell 50000@1.10500,

  `entry_price_avg` for subset 1 = VWAP(1.10000×50000, 1.09900×50000)/100000
  = 1.09950000, matches the test's asserted value; subset 2's re-derived
  `entry_price_avg` = VWAP(1.10500×50000, 1.10800×50000)/100000 =
  1.10650000, matches; `peak_volume` 100000 on both, `realized_pnl`
  650.00000000 (250+400, broker P&L stays attached to its own fill),
  matches. Join happy path (two independently-closed round-trip trades
  merged): traced `assignRoles`' actual role output for the 4-member
  merged sequence — because trade A was already closed before trade B
  opened, `assignRoles`' running-total walk produces roles
  `[entry, exit, add, exit]` (a genuine instance of the "pathological
  sequence" the file's own header flags as a known, accepted, non-corrupting
  limitation for the SPLIT case — here it occurs naturally on JOIN's own
  happy path, not just as a hypothetical). Verified `computeTradeFacts`
  handles this correctly regardless: it classifies members by
  `role === 'entry' || 'add'` vs `'trim' || 'exit'` via `.filter()`, not by
  sequence position, so `entryPriceAvg` = VWAP(2000, 2020) = 2010,
  `exitPriceAvg` = VWAP(2010, 2030) = 2020, `realizedPnl` = 10+10 = 20,
  `peakVolume` = 1 (running total never exceeds 1 in magnitude) — all
  match the test's asserted values exactly, and the arithmetic is
  independently correct, not merely "some value got written." This is a
  reassuring finding in its own right: the filter-based (not
  sequence-based) design in `computeTradeFacts` is robust to exactly the
  kind of odd role ordering a join of two already-closed trades produces.
- **Round-trip test — confirmed it proves something real.** Read
  `split-join.ts`'s own `recomputeGroup`/`assignRoles` logic against the
  round-trip test's assertions: split then re-join of the same two halves
  converges every recomputed fact column (`direction`, `status`,

  `risk_pct`, `initial_risk_pct`, `r_multiple`, `realized_pnl`, `outcome`,
  `hold_seconds`) back to the pre-split values, with only `grouping_source`
  differing (`'user_join'`, as expected) — a real "both operations ran
  AND produced arithmetically-consistent output" proof, not just "neither
  threw."
- **RLS cross-user isolation — genuine, both operations.** Both RLS tests
  use `withUserConnection`'s real `authenticated` role + `auth.uid()`
  resolution (not an app-layer ownership `if`), attempt the operation as a
  second, unrelated real auth user, assert the named not-found error, and

  inside `withUserConnection(userId, ...)`, so a cross-user attempt is
  rejected by Postgres RLS itself (the `WHERE user_id = $2` scoping plus
  the underlying RLS policy both apply), not by an application-level

- **retrospeq-security-reviewer: one blocking FAIL, fixed, re-reviewed
  PASS, 2026-08-22.** The join/delete legitimacy question itself
  (reassign-then-delete vs. a disguised gaming vector) was independently
  re-derived and judged genuinely legitimate: §4.7's "never delete" rule
  exists to stop a trader hiding a decision from analysis, and the
  trigger's own comment frames it that way — join does the opposite,
  recomputing facts over the FULL merged member set so nothing is hidden
  or lost, and the join is bounded to "same block only" so it can't merge
  two genuinely unrelated decisions. The one real, blocking finding: both
  functions' trade-updating UPDATE (inside phase 2) had no atomic guard
  against a concurrent `confirmDay`/`autoConfirmStaleTrades` call
  freezing the trade in the gap between phase 2's own entry
  re-validation SELECT and its later UPDATE — the identical bug class
  already found and fixed in `confirm.ts` earlier this session, left
  unapplied here. Fixed by the orchestrator: `and confirmed_at is null`
  added to both UPDATE WHERE clauses (`splitTrade`'s original-trade
  update, `joinTrades`' survivor update), throwing
  `SplitTradeAlreadyConfirmedError`/`JoinTradeAlreadyConfirmedError` on a
  lost race, positioned before ANY side-effecting work in either function
  (the new-trade insert for split; member reassignment and the
  absorbed-trade delete for join) — a lost race means nothing else in
  that phase-2 call ever runs. Two new deterministic live tests added
  (not `Promise.allSettled` timing luck): a second raw `pg.Client` opens
  an uncommitted confirm-shaped UPDATE on the trade and holds it open,
  forcing the real `splitTrade`/`joinTrades` call to genuinely block on
  the same Postgres row lock — deterministic every run, not dependent on
  JS scheduling. Re-reviewed: PASS — the security-reviewer independently
  judged this technique sounder than the `Promise.allSettled` approach
  used elsewhere, confirmed it exercises the exact fixed code path (not
  an unrelated one), and confirmed the guard placement leaves no
  half-applied write possible in either function (verified against
  `withServiceRoleConnection`'s own `begin`/`commit`/`rollback` wrapping).
- **retrospeq-qa: PASS**, no blocking findings, reviewed with real

- **A real bug found and fixed via the mandatory screenshot/interaction
  self-check, not a code read:** the first version of `NotADecisionToggle.tsx`
  wrapped a `<form action={formAction}>` from `useActionState` around a
  controlled checkbox whose `checked` prop was derived from the action's
  returned `state`, submitted via `formRef.current?.requestSubmit()` on
  the checkbox's own `onChange`. A live-DB-backed Playwright probe
  (`tmp/verify-toggle-persist.mjs`, not committed — throwaway per
  convention) proved the underlying WRITE always succeeded (Postgres
  `not_a_decision` updated correctly both directions), but the checkbox's
  own visual state never updated IN PLACE after a real native click — it
  silently stayed at its pre-click value even once the action had fully
  resolved and the component's own computed `checked` variable had
  genuinely flipped (confirmed via a temporary debug dump). It only ever
  showed correctly after a full page reload (fresh mount). This is the
  documented React gotcha where a checkbox's internal `_valueTracker`
  desyncs once the DOM's `checked` property is toggled by a real user
  click and then reset by React to a *different* value in the same tick
  (exactly what happens while the action is pending) — later updates to
  the same `checked` prop stop reliably reaching the DOM. **Fixed** by
  rewriting the component around local `useState`/`useTransition`
  (optimistic update set synchronously inside the same `onChange` the
  native click fired, rolled back on a server error), calling the Server
  Action directly as a plain async function rather than through a form —
  the standard, reliable pattern for a controlled checkbox, verified
  afterward to flip visually in under 50ms and to persist correctly
  through a reload, both directions, via the same probe script.

    `forbid_frozen_trade_regrouping` trigger's raw, untranslated Postgres
    error instead of the clean named error. Restored immediately after
    confirming.
  - **Real, non-trivial finding: the concurrency-guard test, as originally
    written (100ms fixed `setTimeout` before releasing the raw connection's
    held lock), was NOT actually exercising the atomic guard it claimed to
    prove — for ANY of the three operations in this file (`splitTrade`,
    `joinTrades`, `resolveAmbiguousGroupingAsSingle`), not just the new one.**
    Coverage showed the guarded UPDATE's own `rowCount !== 1` throw branch had
    ZERO hits across the entire test file, including its own dedicated
    concurrency tests. Root cause: in this environment, the cumulative
    round-trip latency of phase 1 + phase 2's own connect/BEGIN/SELECT chain
    routinely exceeds 100ms on its own, so by the time the guarded UPDATE
    is even sent, the racing connection has usually already committed — the
    race gets caught by phase 2's own EARLIER upfront re-validation SELECT
    (a read-then-act check, not the atomic guard) before the guarded UPDATE
    is ever reached. Proven empirically: temporarily removed the atomic
    `and confirmed_at is null` clause from all three guarded UPDATEs in turn
    and reran each operation's own "concurrency guard" test — **all three
    still passed**, meaning none of them were actually proving what their own
    names/comments claimed. **Fixed for `resolveAmbiguousGroupingAsSingle`
    only** (the function under direct review this pass): replaced the fixed
    sleep with a new `waitForBlockedQuery()` helper
    (`lib/ingestion/__tests__/split-join.live.test.ts`) that polls
    `pg_stat_activity` for a backend whose query matches the guarded UPDATE's
    own text and whose `wait_event_type = 'Lock'` — i.e. proof from Postgres
    itself that the guarded UPDATE is genuinely on the lock queue — before
    committing the race connection. Re-verified this new version: passes
    against the real guarded code, and genuinely FAILS (non-tautological)
    when the atomic clause is removed. **`splitTrade`'s and `joinTrades`'
    own concurrency tests have the SAME weakness and were NOT touched by this
    pass** (pre-existing, inherited pattern predating this session's fix, out
    of this narrow review's scope to silently rewrite) — flagging for
    whoever next touches those two tests or does a broader concurrency-test
    audit; they currently prove "some check catches this race" rather than
    "the atomic guard specifically catches this race."
  - **`ResolveAmbiguousGroupingNotAmbiguousError` refusal: confirmed genuine,
    one test gap closed.** The existing test only proved refusal against
    `confident_single`; added a second test proving refusal against
    `confident_split` too (the schema's third `grouping_confidence` value,

    check is a refusal rule specific to it (`splitTrade`/`joinTrades` don't

known-future-needs reference; `NEEDS_YOUR_INPUT.md` is only for things
actually stalling current work. See AGENTS.md → "When something needs
the owner — never fake it, always flag it."

- [ ] **Repo-wide: several RLS INSERT/"for all" policies check `user_id = auth.uid()` but not that referenced foreign keys (`account_id`, `trade_id`, etc.) actually belong to that same user.** Found by retrospeq-security-reviewer (2026-08-22) reviewing Module 02's `fills`/`trade_events` INSERT policies and `trades`/`arm_events`/`trade_captures`'s "for all" policies — a client could theoretically INSERT a row self-assigning `user_id` correctly while pointing `account_id`/`trade_id` at a row it doesn't actually own. Confirmed this is not new to Module 02 — the same shape exists on Module 01's `trading_accounts_owner`/`account_credentials_owner_insert` policies too. Not fixed now (out of scope for the slice that found it, and no test currently proves it's exploitable end-to-end — the referenced row would need to belong to another real user, and the practical blast radius depends on what a client could actually DO with a cross-user-linked row it can't otherwise read, which for most of these tables is "nothing visible," since the owning row still isn't selectable by the attacker afterward). Worth a dedicated pass adding `and exists (select 1 from retrospeq.trading_accounts where id = account_id and user_id = auth.uid())`-shaped checks (or equivalent) across every affected policy, repo-wide, rather than patching table-by-table as each is touched. **Confirmed a further instance, 2026-09-04, Module 03 Slice 03b's own security review**: `field_usages_owner_insert`'s RLS policy doesn't verify `used_by_id` ownership at the RLS layer either — a client could theoretically INSERT a `field_usages` row self-assigning `user_id` correctly while pointing `used_by_id` at a strategy or rule they don't own. - [ ] **A `strategy_var` field's `owner_strategy_id` is never verified to match the strategy actually referencing it in `field_usages` -- a strategy can reference (via `createStrategy`/`editStrategy`) any of the user's own active `strategy_var` fields, not just ones it nominally owns, contrary to §4.2's "that strategy only" scoping for that kind.** Found by `retrospeq-security-reviewer`, 2026-09-09, reviewing Module 03 Slice 03e (field promotion) -- explicitly flagged there as a pre-existing Slice 03b/03c-era gap, not introduced or worsened by promotion's own race analysis. Confirmed directly by `retrospeq-qa`'s own code read the same day: `fetchFieldDefinitionsByIds` (`lib/fields/strategy-repository.ts` L157-176) and `rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy`'s own post-lock precondition guard both check only `user_id` + `state = 'active'` -- neither ever checks `owner_strategy_id` against the strategy actually being saved. **This is a same-user, application-layer scope gap, genuinely distinct from the `field_usages_owner_insert` entry above** (that one is a cross-user RLS gap -- `used_by_id` ownership not verified at the RLS layer; this one is entirely within one user's own data -- a trader's strategy B can silently pick up a `strategy_var` field scoped to their own strategy A). Reconciled and added here per this repo's own Infra-gaps-list convention, since it previously existed only in the 2026-09-09 decision-log entry, not in this durable list.

  ALL as extra positional arguments to vitest -- which broadened what looked
  like a scoped run into an accidental full-repo run every time (explains an
  early false alarm: a "scoped" run showed 209 files/2468 tests, and a

  free machine by serializing dozens of live-DB tests that are normally
  parallelized). Fix: use plain Bash redirection (`> file 2>&1`), not `*>` --
  once corrected, every detection-engine-scoped run finished in ~1-63s with
  zero memory issues. Flagging this explicitly since AGENTS.md's own
  infra-notes template (`C:` `ENOSPC`, etc.) is exactly where a future agent
  hitting the identical false "the suite won't scope/OOMs" conclusion should

     WHERE/EXISTS clause against one consistent read-committed snapshot as
     part of executing this one statement -- there is no window between
     "read to decide" and "delete" for a client (or another request) to
     invalidate. current_version is the one column that actually changes
     when a strategy gains real content (applyStrategyEditVersion's step

     protection). Considered the narrower case of two literally
     concurrent, in-flight (uncommitted) transactions racing for the SAME
     row -- worst case for a same-user self-race (e.g. a second browser
     tab; there is no genuine same-flow concurrency since this function
     only runs sequentially after editStrategy has already failed and
     rolled back) is Postgres's own row-lock serialization causing one
     side to lose and hit the pre-existing "structurally impossible"

     Independent trust-boundary assessment (the actual ask of this
     dispatch): NOT currently exploitable, NOT a live security hole today,
     but a real, correctly-flagged completeness gap with genuine future
     security-adjacent stakes. Reasoning:
     - `grep -rln "detections" app/ lib/` (excluding this slice's own
       files/tests) surfaces exactly two hits -- app/(app)/rules/page.tsx
       (prose comments only, "ranked detections leading," no code reading
       the table) and lib/ingestion/sync.ts (the write-side hook itself).
       There is no downstream reader of the detections table anywhere in
       this repo today. Nothing can currently misuse a count-tier row as a
       rule proposal, because nothing currently reads detections at all
       for that purpose. This is the load-bearing fact for my verdict: an
       absent enforcement point is only actively dangerous if something is
       exercising the gap it should be closing, and nothing is.
     - This is NOT the same as saying it's fine to leave alone. Per
       05-analytics-and-findings.md section 5's own prose (verified
       directly, quoted verbatim in the tester's entry below):
       rule_proposable is described as computed centrally in Module 05
       SPECIFICALLY so downstream consumers (Module 06's rule-proposal
       surface, per section 6.1 of the same spec, "provides -> Findings
       and detections with rule_proposable") never have to re-derive the
       two-field conjunction (tier is count_outcome AND classification is
       pattern) themselves. That conjunction IS mechanically recoverable
       from the persisted tier/classification columns today (both columns
       exist, both are correctly computed and tested per the tester's own
       coverage) -- so a careful future implementation COULD reconstruct
       the identical boolean without the dedicated column. But "correctly
       recoverable if implemented exactly right" is a materially weaker
       guarantee than "computed once, centrally, and impossible to get
       subtly wrong per call site" -- and the specific non-negotiable at
       stake here ("the count tier never proposes a rule on frequency
       alone") is exactly the kind of rule where a single
       off-by-one-field mistake in a future Module 06 dispatch (e.g.
       checking classification alone, forgetting the tier half) would
       silently reintroduce the exact failure mode the spec's own prose
       calls out by name.
     - My verdict: this is a security-relevant, spec-mandated enforcement
       gap that I would block a FUTURE consumer's launch on, but I do NOT
       block THIS slice's own security PASS on it, for three reasons:
       (a) it is not currently exploitable -- no live code path exists to
       misuse it; (b) it is explicitly not mine to fix under this
       dispatch's own constraints (adding rule_proposable is production
       logic -- a new computed field plus a migration column -- squarely a

  3. **ADR 0029 SUPERSESSION KEY -- VERIFIED AGAINST ACTUAL CODE, not
     just trusted from the ADR's own prose.** ADR 0029 claims: key is
     `(user_id, analytic_id)`, enforced by a non-deferrable partial unique
     index (`detections_active_analytic_uidx`), write pattern is
     supersede-then-insert as two separate statements inside one
     `pg_advisory_xact_lock`-guarded transaction (never a combined CTE),
     and a gate-failed analytic's prior `active` row is left untouched.
     Read `repository.ts`'s `writeDetectionsForUser` line by line: it
     locks on the full `(userId, analyticId)` tuple string, then issues an
     UPDATE (state to superseded, where user_id/analytic_id/state=active)
     strictly BEFORE the INSERT (values ending in 'active'), in that
     literal statement order, inside the same client transaction --

      personal threshold) is excluded from `occurrenceTradeIds` -- only
      trades STRICTLY AFTER it count, matching the code's own `i >
      breachedAt` (strict) comparison and the header's "at least one
      FURTHER trade opens ... AFTER the crossing" wording read literally.
      A day whose crossing is only detectable at its own last trade
      therefore never becomes an occurrence at all (no next trade to be
      "further"). Also documented via a dedicated test:
      `computeTradesPerDayOccurrences`'s baseline-MEDIAN-building loop
      excludes a day if ANY trade is in-window, while its candidacy loop
      requires EVERY trade to be in-window for a day to count as a window
      day -- a straddling day is therefore excluded from the median
      computation entirely (confirmed by a dedicated test: an extreme
      20-trade straddling day does not shift a median that should
      otherwise have been unaffected). Neither is asserted as wrong --
      both are internally consistent given how the two loops are
      written -- but both are genuinely non-obvious and are now pinned by
      a named, commented test rather than left to be silently
      rediscovered.

  1. Advisory lock key -- (a) and (c) PASS, (b) FAIL.
     (a) Granularity -- CONFIRMED segment-level, matching the tester own
     "different segments do not over-serialize" finding. Read
     writeFindingsForStrategy directly (repository.ts L363-446): the
     lock key is the string built from userId, strategyId, r.fieldId,
     and JSON.stringify(r.segment), hashed via
     pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1::text)) -- the FULL exact tuple
     the unique index is scoped to, not a coarser field- or
     strategy-level grain. This matches the coder own header comment
     (L302-317) verbatim and explains why the tester own "concurrent
     writers, DIFFERENT segments of the same field" adversarial case
     (search "FULL RE-VERIFICATION" for that result) saw zero lock
     contention -- different segments hash to (almost certainly)
     different keys and were never expected to collide.
     (b) Multi-segment lock-acquisition ordering within one transaction
     -- FAIL, real gap, not present anywhere in this file or its tests.
     withServiceRoleConnection wraps writeFindingsForStrategy entire
     "for (const r of results)" loop in ONE transaction (begin, fn,
     commit -- lib/supabase/direct.ts L60-83) -- pg_advisory_xact_lock is
     transaction-scoped, so every segment this one call touches
     accumulates its own lock, all held until the final commit. This is
     EXACTLY the "single call references MULTIPLE [lock keys] at once"
     shape strategy-repository.ts own rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy
     documents by name (its own "DEADLOCK AVOIDANCE" comment, L246-257)
     as requiring locks be acquired in one CONSISTENT, sorted order
     across every call site -- quoting it directly: acquiring them in
     the caller-supplied (effectively arbitrary) array order would let
     two concurrent calls that both reference the same keys, in opposite
     orders, deadlock. writeFindingsForStrategy does not do this: it
     iterates results in whatever order computeEdgeFindingsForStrategy
     (edge-engine.ts L146, "for (const field of fields)") produced them,
     and fields itself comes from fetchStrategyFieldSpecs own SQL
     (repository.ts L76-79: select id, data_type from retrospeq.fields
     where user_id = $1 and id = any($2::text[]) and state = active)
     with NO order-by clause at all -- confirmed by reading the query
     text directly, not inferred.
     Postgres does not guarantee row order for a query with no ORDER BY;
     two concurrent recomputes of the SAME strategy (the realistic
     scenario this whole fix was built for -- "an overlapping manual
     recompute-now racing a triggered recompute," per this file own
     header) could in principle see that unordered field list come back
     in different orders and therefore acquire their accumulated
     per-segment locks in different orders, which is exactly the
     precondition for a genuine two-transaction deadlock -- neither
     writer can proceed, Postgres own deadlock detector kills one with
     an error. Checked whether anything elsewhere in this call path
     imposes a stable order instead: segmentation.ts own segment
     builders DO sort deterministically WITHIN a field
     (buildPickOneSegments/buildPickManySegments both sort their option
     lists; buildBoolSegments/buildRatingSegments/buildNumberSegments
     all produce a fixed, value-derived order) -- but nothing sorts
     ACROSS fields, which is where the actual gap lives. Also note the
     inconsistency this creates within repository.ts itself: the SAME
     function own header (L338-345) explicitly rejects relying on
     "PostgreSQL explicitly UNSPECIFIED execution order" for the
     unrelated CTE-ordering problem it fixed, calling that reliance
     "the opposite of this codebase own prove-dont-assume posture" --
     yet the field-fetch query row order, which this same function
     lock-acquisition sequence implicitly depends on for
     deadlock-freedom, has exactly the same unproven-assumption shape.
     Severity, reasoned through rather than assumed: this is NOT a
     data-corruption or security defect -- the partial unique index
     remains a genuine backstop regardless (a deadlock just aborts one
     transaction with an error, it does not let two active rows
     through), and the background job self-heals (the post-sync hook
     already wraps this call in a try/catch that logs and moves on,
     sync.ts L1228-1235, and will simply retry cleanly on the next
     sync). But it is a real, previously-untested gap: none of the
     tester own 13 adversarial scenarios exercised "one transaction
     writing MULTIPLE segments while a second concurrent transaction
     writes an overlapping set" -- every scenario tested was same-tuple
     or different-tuple-no-overlap, never the specific "same strategy,
     multiple overlapping segments, transaction-held locks" shape that
     triggers this. Recommended fix, cheap and requires no new round
     trip: sort results by a stable composite key (fieldId then
     JSON.stringify(segment), or equivalently add order by id to
     fetchStrategyFieldSpecs own query) before the for loop in
     writeFindingsForStrategy, mirroring rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy
     own "lockOrderedIds = [...uniqueIds].sort()" pattern exactly.
     (c) Collision reasoning -- re-derived independently for this
     specific lock, PASS. The established low-probability/low-
     consequence reasoning applies unchanged here: hashtext() 32-bit
     output space is shared globally across every pg_advisory_xact_lock
     call site in this repo (archiveField, promoteRuleSeverity,
     rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy, createStrategy, now this write), but
     every one of those call sites actual guarded writes re-check the
     real tuple in their own WHERE clause or a real constraint --
     confirmed for THIS lock specifically: statements 1-3 in
     writeFindingsForStrategy all scope by the literal (user_id,
     strategy_id, field_id, segment) values, never by the hash, so an
     accidental collision with an unrelated lock (this file own key
     format, or a totally different subsystem hashtext call) can only
     ever cause harmless extra serialization -- confirmed, not just
     cited.

  **VERDICT ON THE FALSE-POSITIVE-RATE QUESTION -- REAL DEFECT, NOT A
  CALIBRATION ARTIFACT. BLOCKING.** The coder's own test measured a
  family-wise FPR of 0.0790 against nominal alpha=0.05 (confirmed
  reproduced independently, byte-for-byte same numbers, this session:
  `familyWiseFalsePositiveRate=0.0790 perSegmentFalsePositiveRate=0.0102`)
  and attributed it to "asymptotic test calibration at moderate n" --
  both underlying tests (two-proportion z-test, Welch's t-test) running
  slightly hot. I built a genuinely independent simulation
  (`tmp/fpr_pure_python_sim.py` -- pure Python `math`+`mpmath`, zero
  shared code with `stats.ts`, multinomial segment assignment instead
  of round-robin, correlated win/R generation, variable n=100-300 per
  user, 6000 synthetic no-effect users) that isolates the two
  candidate mechanisms by running the SAME synthetic data through THREE
  variants of the per-segment p-value: `winrate_only` (two-proportion
  z-test alone), `avgr_only` (Welch t-test alone), and `min_combined`
  (the ACTUAL gates.ts behaviour -- `min(pWinRate, pAvgR)` as one
  p-value per segment, per ADR 0025). Result: `winrate_only`
  familyWiseFPR=0.0412 (se=0.0026, at/under nominal), `avgr_only`
  familyWiseFPR=0.0453 (se=0.0027, essentially exactly nominal) --
  **neither individual test is liberal at these sample sizes,
  contradicting the coder's own "asymptotic calibration" explanation
  outright**. `min_combined` familyWiseFPR=0.0658 (se=0.0032, ~4.9
  standard errors above nominal, and ~4-5 SE above BOTH single-test
  variants run on the identical data). A diagnostic fourth variant,
  `min_combined_bonferroni2` (Sidak/Bonferroni-adjusting the pairwise
  minimum -- `min(1, 2*min(pWinRate, pAvgR))` -- before it enters the
  Holm family), brought familyWiseFPR back to 0.0347, under nominal.
  This is the textbook mechanism: `min(p1, p2)` of two not-fully-
  dependent p-values is not itself a valid p-value (its null
  distribution is stochastically smaller than Uniform(0,1) whenever the
  two tests aren't perfectly redundant), and Holm's FWER-control
  guarantee is conditioned on every family member being a valid raw
  p-value -- feeding it an optimistic combined statistic without
  correcting for the implicit "pick the better of two tests" step
  breaks that precondition and inflates the true family-wise error
  rate, exactly as reproduced here on a structurally different
  generative design than the coder's own. **`docs/adr/0025` itself
  states the same unverified "asymptotic test calibration ... not a
  Holm-scoping bug" explanation in its own Consequences section and
  needs a correction** -- the actual root cause IS a consequence of
  ADR 0025's own min-combination design decision, not an unrelated
  asymptotic artifact. Both `holmCorrection` (step-down algorithm
  itself) and `studentTTwoTailedPValue` (the regularized incomplete
  beta function) are independently confirmed CORRECT: `holmCorrection`
  matches hand-worked values on 6 cases including every requested edge
  case (all-above-alpha/nothing-rejects, all-below-alpha/m/everything-
  rejects, exact ties, single-element family, exact boundary
  p=alpha/m); `studentTTwoTailedPValue` matches an arbitrary-precision
  `mpmath` reference (30 decimal digits, a completely independent
  implementation of the regularized incomplete beta function) to 9-10
  significant figures on every spot-checked (t, df) pair. The defect is
  specifically and only in `gates.ts`'s `computeRawPValue` combining
  two per-segment tests into one family member without a multiplicity
  correction on that combination -- not in Holm, not in the individual
  significance tests, not in "moderate-n asymptotics." Recommended fix
  direction (not implemented by this tester -- out of scope for a
  verification pass): Bonferroni/Sidak-adjust the per-segment
  min-of-two before it enters the Holm family (my own diagnostic
  variant demonstrates this closes the gap), or restructure §4.3's
  "OR across two metrics" gate to not require combining two p-values
  into one Holm-family member at all. **This must not proceed to
  security-reviewer/qa until re-coded and re-verified.**

  **CONCURRENCY PROBE -- REAL RACE CONDITION FOUND, BLOCKING.** Ran
  `tmp/edge-engine-concurrency-probe.mjs` against the real live DB
  using the actual `findings` upsert SQL copied verbatim from
  `writeFindingsForStrategy` (`repository.ts`), two genuinely
  concurrent `pg` connections racing to write findings for the SAME
  `(user_id, strategy_id, field_id, segment)` tuple, verified via real
  `pg_stat_activity` lock-wait polling (watchdog DID observe a genuine
  `wait_event_type='Lock'` row during the race -- not a timing guess).
  Result: **TWO simultaneously `state='active'` rows exist for
  `segment={op:'eq',value:true}` after the race** (n=30 and n=32, both
  active, neither superseding the other) -- a direct violation of the
  per-exact-segment-tuple supersession invariant `docs/adr/0024`
  documents. Root cause: `writeFindingsForStrategy`'s single
  insert+update CTE is atomic WITHIN one transaction (ADR 0024's own
  "no window where a crash could leave both rows active" claim is true
  and unaffected) but under READ COMMITTED isolation with no unique
  constraint enforcing "at most one active row per tuple" at the DB
  level (confirmed: no such partial unique index exists on `findings`
  in `20260908010000_analytics_registry_schema.sql`), two CONCURRENT
  transactions' UPDATE steps each only see and supersede rows already
  committed as of their own statement's snapshot -- neither sees the
  other's not-yet-committed INSERT, so both commit as `active`.
  `repository.live.test.ts`'s own "verified live" claim in ADR 0024
  only exercises SEQUENTIAL double-runs, never concurrent ones, so
  this gap was never exercised before. Fix direction (not implemented
  here): a partial unique index on
  `(user_id, strategy_id, field_id, segment) where state = 'active'`
  combined with `ON CONFLICT`-based supersession, or a

  concurrent writers -- same class of fix Module 03 Slice 03d's
  `archiveField` TOCTOU bug used. Realistic trigger scenario: an
  overlapping manual "recompute now" action racing a scheduled/
  triggered recompute for the same strategy. **This must be fixed and

  field to `kind='account'`, setting `owner_strategy_id = null`,

  never a raw Postgres error. New `findPromotionCandidates` -- a

  per §6.1's flow (a second strategy wanting a similarly-named
  `strategy_var` field already scoped to a different strategy),
  reusing `field-validation.ts`'s `normalizeForMatch` (newly exported)
  rather than a second, divergent similarity heuristic -- deliberately
  does not call `promoteField` itself or decide anything unilaterally.

  slice's own dispatch instruction, matching Slice 03d's precedent of
  in-file comments over a new ADR for a spec-interpretation call, not
  a 00-foundation convention deviation): (1) promoting an
  already-`account` field is an idempotent no-op, matching

  field is rejected via the existing immutability trigger, surfaced as

       selectors embed the same pattern inside an esquery attribute
       regex delimited by slashes, which requires literal slash
       characters in the pattern to be escaped so the selector string
       doesn't terminate early -- once that mechanical escaping
       difference is accounted for, the pattern is character-for-
       character identical across all three mechanisms. This is
       necessary context-driven re-escaping, not three independently
       hand-maintained copies that could silently diverge -- confirmed
       by inspection, not by trusting the ADR's own claim that they
       "cannot drift apart."

  4. The 60-second config cache -- "never caches failure state" --
     CONFIRMED TRUE by reading the code directly, not the summary.
     lib/analytics/config-cache.ts's setCachedAnalyticConfig
     (lines 77-84) opens with "if (value.status === 'unavailable')
     return;" before ever touching the Map -- an explicit,
     unconditional early exit, not a conditional that could be
     bypassed. The only two statuses ever written to the cache are
     'found' and 'not_found', both genuine successful reads. A real
     I/O failure (withUserConnection itself throwing inside
     config-repository.ts's getAnalyticConfig) propagates as a thrown
     exception BEFORE execution ever reaches the setCachedAnalyticConfig
     call at the bottom of that function -- confirmed by reading
     config-repository.ts lines 37-95 directly: the try/catch around
     the cache WRITE only wraps the write call itself, not the
     withUserConnection read above it, so a thrown read error exits
     the function entirely via its own unhandled propagation, never
     reaching the cache write at all. Reasoned through both directions
     this dispatch asked for: a caching bug that accidentally cached a
     failure state would, if it happened, be the WORSE direction
     (pinning a possibly-wrong "unavailable" or, worse, a stale-but-
     wrong "found" result for up to 60s past when the real state
     changed) -- but the code structurally cannot do this for the
     'unavailable' case (explicit guard), and the 'found'/'not_found'
     cases it does cache are, by definition, at the point of caching,
     genuinely correct reads, not failures being mistaken for
     successes. No gap found here.

     `findings.user_id` to NULL too, immediately violating its own `not

     cascade` instead, which has no such footgun -- this was the first
     one to attempt `set null`. Fixed using PostgreSQL 15's column-scoped
     `on delete set null (<column>)` syntax (confirmed available -- this
     project's live Postgres is 17.6), which nulls only the named
     column. Verified live, both via the corrected migration DDL and a
     direct `ALTER ... DROP/ADD CONSTRAINT` applied to the already-live
     table to match. Documented at length in the migration itself (a
     future reader attempting the same "composite FK + set null" pattern
     elsewhere in this repo should find this warning before repeating
     the mistake).

       hypothetical `lib/rulesengine/thing` (`../../rulesengine/thing`)
       -- **neither flagged**, confirming the regex's `(/.*)?` /
       end-of-string anchor correctly requires "rules" to be a whole path
       SEGMENT, not merely a substring/prefix of the next segment. No
       false-positive risk from the depth-agnostic regex.
     - A dynamic import built from **runtime string concatenation**
       (`` await import(base + '/operand-catalogue') ``, `base` a
       variable) -- **not caught**, exactly as ADR 0021 itself already
       documents as an accepted, inherent-to-static-analysis residual
       gap. Consistent with the ADR's own claim -- no new finding here.
     - **A dynamic import using a TEMPLATE LITERAL WITH ZERO
       SUBSTITUTIONS** (`` await import(\`@/lib/rules/operand-catalogue\`) ``,
       no `${...}` anywhere in it) -- **NOT CAUGHT. Zero ESLint output,
       exit code 0.** This DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS ADR 0021's own text
       (bypass (a) section): "This selector matches an `ImportExpression`
       whose argument is a string literal **(or template literal with no
       substitutions --** esquery's `.value` attribute lookup only
       resolves for nodes that actually have a static `.value` **...)**"
       -- the ADR's own parenthetical explicitly groups "template literal
       with no substitutions" together with "string literal" as being
       caught. It is not. Root-caused directly against the real parser,
       not just asserted: `espree.parse` on
       `` import(`@/lib/rules/operand-catalogue`) `` produces an
       `ImportExpression` whose `.source` node has `type: "TemplateLiteral"`
       and genuinely **no `.value` property at all** (confirmed via a
       throwaway Node script printing the parsed AST directly) -- `.value`
       is a property that exists on `Literal` nodes (plain
       `'...'`/`"..."` strings) only; a `TemplateLiteral` node's actual
       content lives in its `.quasis[].value.raw`/`.cooked`, a completely
       different shape the current `no-restricted-syntax` selector
       (`ImportExpression[source.value=/pattern/]`) never inspects,
       REGARDLESS of whether the template has zero or more substitutions.
       This is a genuinely easy, innocent-looking bypass -- template
       literals for import specifiers are a common, unremarkable stylistic
       choice in many codebases (especially ones already using template
       literals for path aliases elsewhere), not an obscure evasion
       technique someone would need to go looking for. **This is a real,
       reportable, currently-undocumented gap in the mechanism AGENTS.md
       names as a repo-wide non-negotiable ("enforce in CI, not just
       review") -- flagged here for `retrospeq-security-reviewer` to
       weigh in on explicitly before this slice's ESLint boundary is

       selector matching `ImportExpression[source.type='TemplateLiteral']`
       with a `.quasis` length/content check (or, more simply, a selector
       that flags ANY `ImportExpression` whose source is a

       reasoning that a dynamic import under this specific boundary
       having a legitimate reason to use a template literal at all is
       vanishingly unlikely) -- not attempted here, since this dispatch's

       pass; recorded as a finding for the next coder dispatch to close,
       matching item 3's own already-established "found, not silently

- 2026-09-08 -- SECURITY REVIEW GATE, Module 03 Slice 03d (field
  LIFECYCLE, §4.5 rename/archive), the concurrency-fix build the two
  2026-09-08 entries below this one describe and the second-pass
  independent re-verification above them already covered end to end.
  This is the security-reviewer's OWN dedicated gate, per its dispatch's
  explicit framing -- blocking authority, does not re-trust the tester's
  own re-verification for items it can independently check itself.
  **PASS on all 5 focus items**, verified by direct code reading
  (`lib/fields/strategy-repository.ts`, `lib/fields/fields-repository.ts`,
  `supabase/migrations/20260902010000_field_registry_schema.sql`,
  `lib/supabase/direct.ts`) plus live-DB test re-execution, not by
  trusting either the coder's fix report or the tester's own two
  independent-verification passes:
  1. **Advisory-lock key-choice collision analysis -- PASS, no
     correctness risk, confirmed beyond what the prior reviews already
     established.** Confirmed directly: every `pg_advisory_xact_lock`
     call site in this repo (`strategy-repository.ts` L277 and
     `fields-repository.ts` L931, both field-id-keyed; `severity-
     lifecycle-repository.ts` L230 and `rules-repository.ts` L333, both
     user-id-keyed) uses the single-`bigint`-argument overload
     (`hashtext(...)` returns `int4`, implicitly widened to `bigint`),
     never the two-`int`-argument form -- so all four call sites genuinely
     share ONE Postgres advisory-lock keyspace (Postgres's own lock-tag
     internals give the single-bigint form and the two-int form disjoint
     `objsubid` tags; this repo never uses the latter, so that potential
     escape hatch is moot -- everything here really is one space).
     `hashtext()` hashes raw bytes with no knowledge of the caller's
     intended "kind" of string, so a `fields.id` (`'acct.<uuidv7>'`/
     `'str.<uuidv7>'`) colliding with an unrelated `profiles.id` UUID
     string's hash is possible in principle -- probability ~1/2^32 per
     specific pair, the same order of magnitude the repo's own prior
     reviews (Slice 10b's security-reviewer pass, PROGRESS.md L3483-3499;
     this slice's own first- and second-pass tester re-verifications,
     L8718-8727) already accepted for the user-id-only keyspace, now
     re-confirmed to still hold with a THIRD keyspace (field ids) added.
     Consequence, independently re-derived rather than re-quoted: harmless
     extra serialization at worst, NEVER a correctness or authorization
     problem, because advisory locks grant no access of their own -- every
     guarded UPDATE/INSERT this repo pairs with a lock (`archiveField`'s
     `where ... state = 'active' and not exists (...)`,
     `rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy`'s post-lock state re-check,
     `promoteRuleSeverity`'s/`insertRuleAndVersion`'s own count guards)
     still re-checks the REAL id/user_id in its own WHERE clause regardless
     of which lock number was acquired to get there.
     Went one step further than the prior reviews by checking the ONE new
     wrinkle this slice introduces that neither Slice 10b's review nor the
     tester's own re-verification explicitly traced: within a SINGLE
     transaction, `insertStrategyAndVersion` (`strategy-repository.ts`
     L495) acquires a user-id lock FIRST, then -- still inside the same
     transaction, before commit -- calls `rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy`
     (L533), which acquires one or more field-id locks. Confirmed by
     reading every call site in the repo that this is the ONLY function
     that ever holds two DIFFERENT advisory-lock keyspaces open at once,
     and confirmed the ordering is fixed and one-directional everywhere:
     no code path acquires a field-id lock and then attempts a user-id
     lock (`archiveField` acquires exactly one lock, its own field's,
     ever; `applyStrategyEditVersion` acquires field-id locks only, no
     user-id lock at all). A real (non-collision) deadlock between the two
     keyspaces is therefore impossible by construction -- standard
     lock-ordering discipline, one direction only, everywhere. Even in the
     astronomically unlikely double-coincidence case (two independent
     ~1/2^32 collisions lining up to form an actual wait-for cycle across
     two concurrent transactions), Postgres's own deadlock detector (runs
     every ~1s by default) would abort one side with a `deadlock_detected`
     error rather than hang -- worst case is a transient, retryable
     failure on a vanishingly rare coincidence, never silent corruption or
     an authorization bypass. Confirms Slice 10b's own prior conclusion
     ("no cycle is possible... neither ever holds a second lock while
     waiting on another") still holds for the narrower two-user-id-lock-
     sites case it was written about, and extends the same reasoning
     (this review's own, not merely restated) to now cover the field-id
     keyspace and the one new same-transaction nesting case this slice
     actually introduces.
  2. **Lock-input provenance -- PASS, both call sites hash a
     server-validated, immutable field id, never raw client input.**
     `archiveField(userId, fieldId)` (`fields-repository.ts` L908-931):
     confirmed the `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1::text))` statement
     at L931 only ever runs AFTER `fetchFieldForLifecycleOp` (L909) has
     already confirmed `fieldId` resolves to a real row owned by this
     `userId` (throws `FieldRecordNotFoundError` otherwise, L910-912) and
     after the dependents pre-check (L920-923) -- a caller cannot reach
     the lock statement with an arbitrary, non-existent string; the only
     "choice" a hostile caller retains is which of their OWN real field
     ids to name, which is already-authorized access, not a lock-key
     injection. `rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy`'s field-id list
     (`strategy-repository.ts` L258-277) is sourced from
     `input.fields.map(f => f.fieldId)` in both `insertStrategyAndVersion`
     and `applyStrategyEditVersion`, but by the time either reaches that
     call, `createStrategy`/`editStrategy` have already run
     `fetchFieldDefinitionsByIds` (scoped `user_id = $1 and state =
     'active'`) and `validateCaptureMoments`, which throws
     `FieldNotFoundError` (`strategy-validation.ts` L190-193) for any
     `fieldId` absent from that user-scoped map -- confirmed by direct
     read, not assumed. Every field id ever hashed is therefore always a
     real `fields.id` value, server-generated once at `createField` time
     via `retrospeq.uuid_generate_v7()` (`fields-repository.ts` L440) and

     stable"). At worst a DoS-adjacent concern (a hostile caller could in
     principle brute-force a string that hashes to a target 32-bit value

  1. **TOCTOU probe against `archiveField`'s guarded UPDATE -- REAL GAP
     FOUND, empirically reproduced against the live DB, not simulated.**
     Read the guarded UPDATE's own SQL first (`... where state = 'active'
     and not exists (select 1 from field_usages ...) returning archived_at`)
     before attempting to defeat it, per this dispatch's own instruction.
     Checked Postgres's own row-lock conflict matrix BEFORE writing a test
     (not assumed): `field_usages(user_id, field_id) references fields
     (user_id, id)` makes an INSERT into `field_usages` take a `FOR KEY
     SHARE` tuple lock on the referenced `fields` row; the guarded UPDATE
     (touching only `state`/`archived_at`, neither part of the PK) takes a
     `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` tuple lock -- and `FOR KEY SHARE` does NOT conflict
     with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` in Postgres's own lock matrix. Net effect:
     there is no lock contention between the two statements at all, so
     `waitForBlockedQuery`/`pg_stat_activity`-polling (this session's usual
     "genuine two-connection" technique, `strategy-repository.live.test.ts`'s
     own precedent) has nothing to observe -- confirmed this is a real
     structural fact about the two statements, not a limitation of the test
     technique. Built the race the only way it can actually be proven
     instead: a real second `pg` connection opens `begin`, inserts a real
     `field_usages` row (replaying the exact statement
     `rebuildFieldUsagesForStrategy` issues, referencing a REAL, previously
     committed `createStrategy` strategy) and holds it UNCOMMITTED, while
     the real `archiveField(...)` call runs concurrently on its own
     connection, then commits the held insert and inspects final state.
     **Empirical, reproducible result:** `archiveField` completes
     successfully (does not throw `FieldInUseError`) because its own
     UPDATE's MVCC snapshot (taken at that statement's own start, READ
     COMMITTED) cannot see the still-uncommitted `field_usages` row -- the
     `not exists` check passes, the archive commits, and the `field_usages`
     insert goes on to commit for real moments later. Final DB state
     confirmed directly (not inferred): `fields.state = 'archived'` AND a
     live, committed `field_usages` row referencing that same field both
     exist simultaneously -- exactly the inconsistency this dispatch asked
     the probe to look for ("a field ending up archived WHILE a strategy
     still references it"). **This is a real gap, not a false alarm**: the

- 2026-09-02 — **Fixed the critical, real account-erasure regression
  Slice 03a's own independent verification found (see the Phase 3 row and
  "Current task" — this entry supersedes both once merged): real GDPR
  hard-delete (`lib/privacy/erasure.ts`'s `executeErasure`) was broken for
  every single user, from the moment `20260902010000_field_registry
  _schema.sql` shipped, because `fields` was never explicitly deleted.**
  Root cause (already diagnosed correctly before this fix was dispatched):
  `fields_forbid_derived_delete`'s `BEFORE DELETE` trigger rejects
  deleting any `kind = 'derived'` row unless
  `retrospeq.erasure_in_progress` is set on the SAME connection issuing
  the delete; every user has 9 permanent derived rows from signup;
  `executeErasure` never explicitly deleted `fields`, relying instead on
  the final `auth.admin.deleteUser` call's GoTrue-side cascade — but
  GoTrue runs that cascade on its OWN, separate Postgres connection, which
  never had the (transaction-local) flag set. Fix: new
  `lib/fields/fields-repository.ts`'s `deleteAllFieldsForUser`, mirroring
  `lib/broker/accounts-repository.ts`'s `deleteAllTradingAccountsForUser`
  exactly (same architecture — `withServiceRoleConnection`, `set_config`
  first, explicit delete, same erasure escape-hatch mechanism), wired into
  `executeErasure`'s step-3b explicit delete list
  (docs/adr/0010-erasure-explicit-delete-order.md, now updated with a
  2026-09-02 addendum documenting both this fix and a second,
  **deliberately NOT fixed here**, instance of the identical bug class:
  `retrospeq.rules`/`retrospeq.rule_evaluations` (Module 04,
  2026-08-23) have the same `erasure_in_progress`-gated `BEFORE DELETE`
  triggers, and `executeErasure` has never explicitly deleted either —
  meaning any user with at least one authored rule almost certainly hits
  the identical failure today, undetected because
  `erasure.live.test.ts` has never seeded a `rules` row. Flagged, not
  silently patched (out of this fix's own explicitly scoped dispatch) —
  needs its own `deleteAllRulesForUser`-shaped follow-up.** Verified:
  `erasure.live.test.ts` 7/7 passing (the original 6, one extended with
  explicit `fields`-count before/after assertions, plus one brand-new
  dedicated regression test proving the exact previously-broken scenario:
  a real user with 9 derived fields, `auth.admin.deleteUser` genuinely
  succeeding where it used to throw); Slice 03a's own 41/42 (1 skipped)

  `trades-freeze-trigger.live.test.ts` timeout (this repo's own

  by its CURRENT rendered sentence, not the wording live during the

  `adherence_weekly` (Slice 6) stores only `top_break_rule_id`, never a

- 2026-08-29 — **Slice 10b's cross-tab `rules.create` cap race (found by
  `retrospeq-tester`'s independent verification) fixed by moving the cap
  guard INTO `insertRuleAndVersion`'s own transaction, not by adding a
  second check to `createRule`.** Same reasoning Slice 7's own
  `promoteRuleSeverity` fix already established for the analogous
  `rules.hard` cap: a two-step "check the count, then write" is
  structurally racy under READ COMMITTED regardless of where the check
  lives, because a correlated `count(*)` subquery only ever observes
  committed rows, never a concurrent transaction's own uncommitted write.
  The fix is `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(user_id))` as
  `insertRuleAndVersion`'s first statement, serializing concurrent
  creates for the SAME user before its own guarded `insert ... select ...
  where (select count(*) ...) < capLimit` runs — not a second entitlement
  check bolted onto `createRule`, which would still race the same way.
  `createRule`'s existing early `canForUser` pre-check is kept exactly as
  it was (fast, friendly, non-atomic, for the common non-racing case);
  the guarded INSERT is the real backstop. `InsertRuleInput.capLimit:
  number | null` (`null` = Pro's unlimited cap, mirroring
  `resolveQuantityCapability`'s own `limit === null` convention) is
  sourced from the SAME `entitlement.limit` the pre-check already
  computed, never a second independently-derived number. See "→ Module
  04 Slice 10b — CODER concurrency fix" in "Current task" above for the
  full verification write-up (tripwire E2E now green, new two-connection
  live-DB proof, Slice 10a regression-checked).

- 2026-08-29 — **Slice 10a's threshold-seeding chose the trader's own
  80th-percentile history (direction-aware) over the raw median, and a
  bounds-midpoint fallback over any other guess when history is
  insufficient.** Reasoning (not obvious from §5.10's own one-line
  "thresholds seeded from `operand_distributions`"): seeding at the raw
  median (p50) would flag roughly HALF the trader's own past trades on
  day one for a rule they didn't even choose to author — punitive, not

  the seeded rule's own would-have-flagged ratio inside `preview.ts`'s
  ALREADY-established "healthy" band (0.06–0.35), reusing that existing
  judgment rather than inventing an unrelated second number. Implemented
  by generalizing `preview.ts`'s private `weightedMedian` into an
  exported `percentileFromBuckets(buckets, p)` (p50 convenience wrapper
  kept, now implemented in terms of the generic function — one walk over
  `DistributionBucket[]`, not two).
